title: Eurotrip
full_review:
Just when you thought that studio stiff shirts couldn't stoop any lower into the bowels of bad taste, you discover that Tinseltown's gutter has a trap door. Such is the case with director Jeff Schaffer's smutty "Eurotrip" (Dreamworks), a relentlessly raunchy so-called comedy about a quartet of high-school friends let loose in Europe in search of good times -- which on this sleazy teen trek means more lust than Louvre.

Dignifying such garbage with any more ink than is absolutely necessary would be almost as much of a waste as the film itself. So, to keep a dumb premise short, the, er, plot involves Scott Thomas (Scott Mechlowicz), a sad-sack senior dumped by his trampy girlfriend (Kristin Kreuk) on graduation day. Wallowing in misery, Scott cries on the cyber-shoulder of his longtime, Berlin-based, computer pen pal Mieke, who he thinks is a guy. When Mieke makes an online pass at him, Scott freaks out and severs the long-distance friendship with a nasty e-mail, only to later discover that Mieke is, in fact, a girl (Jessica Boehrs) -- and gorgeous to boot.

Hoping for a second chance at love, or at least lust, Scott, along with his libidinous lackey, Cooper (Jacob Pitts), hops a jet to Europe where they meet up with two other classmates: Jenny (Michelle Trachtenberg) and her brainy twin brother, Jamie (Travis Wester). Together they embark on a raucous road trip across the continent, exposing themselves, in the words of the press notes, "to every lascivious, larcenous and lecherous indulgence Europe has to offer." Needless to say, their sense of self-dignity doesn't make it through customs.

Given the fact that the vulgarians behind "Eurotrip" are also responsible for such lowest-common-denominator fare as "Road Trip" and "Old School," the puerile parade of debauchery that unfolds shouldn't come as much of a surprise to anyone. Included in the sleazy barrage are scenes involving foul-mouthed English soccer hooligans, an Italian pervert, an incestuous encounter, a kinky Amsterdam S&M parlor and a French nude beach complete with fully naked bathers.

And while such gratuitous lewdness could be dismissed with a disgusted sigh, Schaffer crosses the line from offensive indecency to appalling insensitivity when the raunchy road trip hits Rome. During a severely unfunny sequence at the Vatican, the filmmaker shows a callous disregard for Catholic viewers by incorporating a crucifix hanging in the papal residence into the foursome's irreverent antics. But Schaffer sinks to new lows of profanity by including in the film a racy sex scene which takes place in a confessional.

On a different -- but equally disturbing -- front, Schaffer asks viewers to find humor in Mieke's toddler brother smearing crayon under his nose and marching around the room like Hitler, arm extended in a Nazi salute. Since when did desecrating sacraments and mimicking genocidal maniacs become funny? Dreamworks executives should be ashamed of themselves.

Any way you look at it, "Eurotrip" is nothing more than Eurotrash.

Due to several raunchy sexual encounters, including a sacrilegious sequence, recurring full and partial nudity, drug content, as well as much crude language and humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
